paper_title: WaveGen: Truly End-to-End Waveform Generation via Internal Spectral Trajectory Learning

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: This work proposes WaveGen, a fully end-to-end diffusion-based text-to-waveform framework based on Spectral Forcing, which jointly learns an internal spectral trajectory and the target waveform trajectory within a single model, enabling direct end-to-end text-to-waveform generation. Unlike recent TTS pipelines, WaveGen does not rely on separately trained or externally decoded intermediate representations, such as neural audio codecs, Mel-spectrogram vocoders, or VAE-based latent models. In addition, WaveGen performs internal text-speech alignment within a single model, eliminating the need for external alignment modules such as duration predictors. To preserve a truly end-to-end formulation, our framework further avoids dependence on self-supervised representations, such as BERT-based text embeddings and Wav2Vec 2.0-based semantic representations, as well as semantic distillation methods for training optimization. To achieve this, we carefully design Spectral Forcing, a model architecture with disentangled diffusion heads, and a training objective based on a multi-scale spectral $v$-loss. We further validate the scalability of end-to-end TTS models by scaling the model size from 0.1B to 0.6B parameters. Using a single architecture, open-source data, and one-stage training, without external modules such as duration predictor or REPA, WaveGen demonstrates fully end-to-end waveform generation achieving state-of-the-art performance on the Emilia training dataset. In particular, WaveGen achieves a WER of 1.47 and a SIM of 0.75 on the Seed-en benchmark. Source code and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/sh-lee-prml/WaveGen

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Recent progress in language models and generative models has substantially advanced text-tospeech (TTS) synthesis. Large language model (LLM)-based TTS systems [58, 22] have replaced conventional acoustic representations with neural audio codecs, enabling speech generation through discrete token modeling and in-context voice prompting. In parallel, diffusion and conditional flow matching (CFM)-based TTS models [33, 5] have improved the quality and flexibility of Melspectrogram generation through masked infilling and zero-shot voice conditioning. More recently, latent diffusion approaches [75, 47] further improve the efficiency of generative modeling by operating in compressed representation spaces rather than directly modeling high-dimensional audio signals. Despite these advances, most recent TTS systems still rely on intermediate representations and external waveform decoders. Codec-based models [7, 6, 57] depend on the capacity and quality of neural audio codecs [72, 8, 32, 23, 70, 10, 63, 11]; Mel-spectrogram-based models require separately Equal contribution. Corresponding author: Sang-Hoon Lee (sanghoonlee@ajou.ac.kr) 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). trained neural vocoders; and latent diffusion models require an additional pre-trained latent. These intermediate modules have been highly effective in practice, but they also introduce additional training stages, architectural dependencies, and upper-bound constraints on the final quality. In particular, high-fidelity waveform generation often requires GAN training, carefully designed architectures, or representation-specific optimization, making the overall pipeline increasingly complex. Meanwhile, although end-to-end (E2E) TTS models [53, 26, 12] were explored in earlier studies, their limited scalability, training instability, and inferior zero-shot quality led the field to converge toward multi-stage pipelines. These limitations stem from the high temporal resolution of raw waveforms, which makes text-speech alignment difficult and often requires complex adversarial training for perceptually realistic waveform generation. Only E3-TTS [17] demonstrated the potential of waveform-level diffusion for TTS. However, it still relies on BERT-based text representations to facilitate text-waveform alignment, and directly applying diffusion modeling to waveform signals imposes substantial computational burden due to the high temporal resolution of audio. In this work, we propose WaveGen, fully E2E diffusion-based text-to-waveform framework built upon Spectral Forcing. WaveGen directly generates high-resolution waveform from text within single architecture. The key idea is to revisit the prediction and loss spaces of CFM for raw waveform generation. We found x-prediction with v-loss is essential for E2E waveform generation. Instead of forcing the model to learn waveform dynamics alone, Spectral Forcing jointly guides the model to learn an internal spectral trajectory while optimizing the target waveform trajectory. This design provides structured inductive bias for high-resolution audio generation while preserving truly E2E text-to-waveform formulation. To this end, we carefully design WaveGen architecture with disentangled diffusion heads and introduce multi-scale spectral loss for stable waveform-level flow matching. We further investigate the scalability of E2E TTS by increasing the model size from 0.1B to 0.6B parameters, showing that direct text-to-waveform generation can benefit from model scaling when the training objective and architecture are properly designed. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We propose WaveGen, fully E2E text-to-waveform framework that directly generates raw waveform from text without separately trained intermediate representations. We introduce Spectral Forcing, which jointly learns an internal spectral trajectory and the target waveform trajectory, enabling stable CFM-based optimization in the high-resolution waveform domain. We investigate prediction and loss spaces for waveform generation and design scalable waveform-level diffusion architecture with disentangled diffusion heads. We demonstrate that WaveGen achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot TTS performance using single architecture, open-source data, and one-stage training, providing evidence that fully E2E text-to-waveform generation can be viable alternative to increasingly complex multi-stage TTS pipelines.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: 2.1 Conventional TTS Traditional TTS systems consist of an acoustic model and neural vocoder. Acoustic models generate acoustic features such as Mel-spectrogram, and neural vocoders convert acoustic features into raw waveform signals. Tacotron [64] paved the way of deep-learning based TTS system by introducing attention-based encoder-decoder structure to align text with speech, and Tacotron 2 [55] utilized WaveNet [44] to generate waveform from synthetic Mel-spectrogram. Transformer TTS [40] verified the effectiveness of encoder-decoder Transformer. However, these models suffer from unstable attention alignment and slow inference speed due to their autoregressive (AR) nature. To address these issues, FastSpeech [52] introduced parallel synthesis using duration which is extracted from teacher AR models. Also, GAN-based neural vocoders accelerated TTS research in terms of both quality and inference speed. Specifically, PWG [67] and MelGAN [31] introduced GAN-based vocoder, and HiFi-GAN [29] introduced multi-period discriminator (MPD) which significantly enhances perceptual quality of synthetic speech. BigVGAN [35] scaled up the neural vocoder via snake periodic activation and an anti-aliasing low-pass filter. iSTFTNet [24] and Vocos [56] enhance the sampling efficiency by modeling features in low-resolution space with iSTFT. 2 Table 1: Comparison of WaveGen with recent TTS systems. Then, VALL-E [58] demonstrated neural codec language models can be strong zero-shot TTS system with large-scale training and speech-level prompting. UniAudio [68] and Moshi [9] proposed efficient RVQ decoding method using multi-scale Transformer. Recently, most models utilize pre-trained LLM for TTS backbone, and finetuned them to decode semantic token [13, 14] or RVQ tokens [27, 22, 18] which are extracted from large-scale high-quality audio codec via multi-token prediction (MTP) AR Transformer. Metis [62] and OmniVoice [78] employ discrete diffusion language model using bidirectional Transformer. Diffusion/CFM Grad-TTS [49] demonstrated the effectiveness of diffusion models for TTS. VoiceBox [33] and P-Flow [28] propose CFM-based TTS models via masked-infilling training strategy, which significantly improve zero-shot speech synthesis through speech prompting. E2-TTS [15] introduces novel text-speech alignment learning with filler tokens. F5-TTS [5] and ZipVoice [77] introduce efficient CFM-based TTS models without any external duration predictor. Also, hybrid models such as CosyVoice [13, 14] utilized CFM-based Mel-spectrogram decoder conditioned on semantic tokens. Meanwhile, latent diffusion models (LDM) [34] have been investigated for efficient TTS modeling. Furthermore, continuous language models such as VoxCPM [75] and VibeVoice [47] show their effectiveness of AR diffusion via highly-compressed latent representation. 2.2 End-to-End TTS E2E TTS has long been investigated as way to simplify conventional cascaded speech synthesis pipelines. Early neural TTS systems such as Tacotron [64] established unified sequence-to-sequence framework for text-to-acoustic modeling, but still required Griffin-Lim algorithm [19]. ClariNet [48] explored parallel waveform generation through knowledge distillation from autoregressive WaveNet models. FastSpeech 2s [53] extended non-autoregressive TTS toward direct waveform generation. EATS [12] jointly optimized learnable duration modeling and waveform generation with adversarial training. VITS [26] introduced strong text-to-waveform framework by combining variational inference, normalizing flows [25], and adversarial waveform training [29]. Despite these advances, prior E2E TTS systems still have important limitations: many rely on adversarial training to obtain perceptually realistic waveforms, which require carefully designed multiple discriminators, auxiliary losses, and significantly long training. More importantly, most of these models were not primarily designed for zero-shot speech synthesis, where the model must generate high-quality speech for unseen speakers from text and speech prompts. As result, recent zero-shot TTS research has largely shifted toward codec-based language models, Mel-spectrogram diffusion models, or LDM rather than direct waveform-level generation. Recently, E3-TTS [17] revisited diffusion-based text-to-waveform generation, demonstrating the potential of waveform-level generative modeling for TTS; however, it still relies on pretrained BERTbased text representations to facilitate text-waveform alignment, and directly applying diffusion modeling to high-resolution waveform signals introduces substantial computational cost. In contrast, this paper revisits fully E2E TTS under stricter formulation: single model directly generates waveform from text without neural audio codecs, Mel-spectrogram decoders, VAE, neural vocoders, duration predictors, self-supervised representations, or adversarial training as indicated in Table 1. 3 Figure 1: E2E text-to-waveform diffusion training details. 3 WaveGen
In this paper, we propose a fully E2E single-stage diffusion-based text-to-waveform generative model
as illustrated in Figure 1. We analyze raw waveform as generative targets (Section 3.1), introduce a
novel framework (Section 3.2), and efficient architecture (Section 3.3). Also, we revisit the prediction
space and loss space for raw waveform (Section 3.4) and introduce the improved loss (Section 3.5).
sections.content: 3.1 CFM-based Waveform Generation Recently, diffusion and CFM-based waveform generation models [54, 65, 38, 36] have emerged as promising alternative to GAN-based models, offering new direction for high-fidelity speech synthesis. PeriodWave [39] introduced CFM-based periodic-aware generator for waveform generation. RFWave [42] presented efficient CFM-based models with STFT/iSTFT. Flow2GAN [69] improved CFM objective of waveform in spectral space. StreamFlow [6] proposed streaming flow matching for streaming waveform generation and efficient waveform diffusion Transformers using linear-reshape transformation. However, these works only employ waveform-level diffusion with strongly aligned acoustic conditions such as Mel-spectrogram or pre-trained neural audio codec. In our study, basic CFMs fail to align text-speech in high-resolution waveform space without any external modules. 3.2 Spectral Forcing Due to the difficulty of waveform-level generation, previous works utilize intermediate representations such as Mel-spectrogram. To bridge the gap between text and waveform, we introduce Spectral Forcing, method to jointly learn an internal spectral trajectory and the target waveform trajectory, enabling stable CFM-based optimization in the high-resolution waveform space. Specifically, we introduce low-resolution spectral trajectory as an auxiliary generation target, which provides structured inductive bias for text-speech alignment. Unlike cascaded approaches, the spectral trajectory is jointly generated within the same model and is used only as internal frequency-rich guidance, rather than as an external intermediate representation. We adopt simple DiT [45]-only architecture with AdaLN-SOLA [20]. The model takes as input and its noisy spectral representation xspec the concatenation of the reshaped noisy waveform xwave which is lower-resolution Mel-spectrogram with 64 bins. For text conditioning, we adopt average pooling of ZipVoice [77, 76] that expands the average-pooled text embeddings along the temporal dimension to match the speech length without any external encoder. Following [33, 5], we utilize masked-infilling training for prompted generation by concatenating masked representations together. 3.3 Disentangled DiT Heads We found that concatenating input representations is necessary for better text-speech alignment, but disentangling DiT heads for each representation is required for robust estimation. We use shared DiT blocks as an alignment backbone, and simply add shallow disentangled DiT heads as representationspecific generation. Baseline model uses 14 shared DiT blocks and two disentangled heads. We only compute the loss on the masked regions of the target representation. 4 3.4 Decoupled Prediction and Loss Spaces for Raw Waveform Generation Recent flow matching-based waveform reconstruction models, such as PeriodWave [39] and RFWave [42], have demonstrated the potential of flow-based models for raw waveform reconstruction by improving periodic modeling and sampling efficiency. Despite these advances, we observe that conventional velocity-based objectives can be insufficient for preserving fine-grained waveform energy, often leading to degraded perceptual quality in generated audio. sections.title: 4 Experiment and Result
sections.content: 4.1 Experimental Setup Dataset For small-scale TTS and ablation studies, we utilized LibriTTS (CC-BY-4.0) [73]. LibriTTS is high-quality speech dataset with sampling rate of 24,000 Hz in WAV format. We filtered LibriTTS to include only utterances with durations of up to 12s for efficient training (319,627 samples). For large-scale training, WaveGen-S/B (v0.1) use the English subsets of Emilia (CC-BYNC-4.0) and Emilia-YODAS (CC-BY-4.0) [21] provided as MP3-compressed audio with sampling rate of 24,000 Hz. Following [5], we filter out several speakers and use utterances with durations of up to 30s. We also released WaveGen (0.6B) trained with multilingual Emilia datasets. Training We train LibriTTS models with learning rate of 1104 using the AdamW optimizer [43], fixed batch size of 128 for 1.1M steps. We train Emilia models with learning rate of 1104 using AdamW optimizer [43], dynamic batch size with total 480s frame of waveform for 1.1M steps. All models except for the 0.6B models are trained on four GPUs using mixed precision. Due to limited computational resources, we train the models only for four epochs. We train WaveGen (0.6B) on eight GPUs for 11 epochs. During training, we use masked-infilling strategy by dropping the speech prompt and text condition (0.3 and 0.2, respectively). Sampling We adopt the Euler method as the ODE solver. For CFG scheduling, we build upon the strategy used in ZipVoice, where the text condition is dropped only at early time steps, and all ablation studies are conducted using this. However, when using threshold of < 0.5, we found that this substantially degrades speaker similarity in our model. Therefore, we restrict text-condition dropout to < 0.02. We fix NFE to 32 and CFG to 2 in our experiments. 4.2 Zero-shot TTS results We evaluate zero-shot TTS performance on the Seed-en benchmark dataset [1]. We compute WER and SIM to assess speech intelligibility and speaker similarity using Whisper and WavLM-Large, respectively. Table 2 demonstrates the effectiveness of E2E TTS training without relying on external modules, and shows the scalability of the proposed models by achieving promising performance compared to large-scale TTS systems that require multi-stage training. We also conduct subjective evaluation using Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk) with details provided in Appendix D. We compare WaveGen with publicly available strong baselines, including F5-TTS [5], CosyVoice3 [14], and Qwen3-TTS [22]. Notably, our model achieves comparable mean opinion scores (MOS) for both naturalness (nMOS) and similarity (sMOS) as reported in Table 3. We encourage readers to listen to the audio samples on our demo page. Unlike neural vocoders, E2E TTS models cannot rely on ground-truth spectral inputs during generation. 4.10 Multilingual TTS results
We conduct large-scale multilingual TTS experiments on the English (En) and Chinese (Zh) subsets
of the Emilia dataset, and adopt F5-TTS-based architectures including ConvNeXt-based text encoder
and filler token-based conditioning and hyperparameters of WavTTS including waveform scaling and
time scheduling for fair comparison.2 Table 12 shows that WaveGen achieves strong performance
across all evaluation metrics, demonstrating the effectiveness of direct waveform modeling and
spectral forcing. Specifically, WaveGen achieves speaker similarities of 0.75 and 0.80 on the seed-
en and seed-zh benchmark using only the publicly available Emilia dataset. Notably, we do not
employ REPA when training WaveGen, suggesting further room for improvement through additional
representation alignment techniques. In the following subsections and Appendix F, we further provide
detailed analyses of the waveform diffusion optimization techniques used in WaveGen.
sections.content: Information bottleneck pre-net for multi-representation generation 4.11 We further investigate the effect of Spectral Forcing during large-scale training. When using large-scale dataset, the dependency of Spectral Forcing increases because the model has difficulty aligning text with speech at the initial stage. While Spectral Forcing is weak guidance, the model is prone to learn to reconstruct waveforms from Spectral Forcing, resulting in delayed emergence of text-speech alignment. To reduce this limitation, we revisit the simple techniques, pre-net used in Tacotron [64] by adding information bottleneck layers with two MLP layers and dropout to reduce dependency on teacher forcing for AR training. Specifically, we utilize 8n Mel bins and smaller bottleneck dimension of 32 similar to [3]. We apply this bottleneck layer with dropout of 0.2 during training and inference. It improves the robustness of multi-representation generation by learning to generate waveform from multiple conditions. We investigated the effect of dropout ratio on Spectral Forcing in Appendix F.2. 4.12 Prompt Anchor Following [66], we observe train-inference mismatch in iterative generation under masked-infilling training. During training, the prompt region is fixed to the GT speech and is therefore not explicitly optimized for iterative updates. At inference time, however, repeatedly updating xt in the prompt region can introduce undesirable deviations from the GT prompt trajectory. To address this issue, we anchor the prompt region to GT-based intermediate state during iterative sampling. Specifically, at each sampling step, we construct the prompt-region xt by interpolating between the corresponding x0 and x1, rather than using the model-updated values. This simple prompt anchoring strategy substantially improves speaker similarity by reducing the train-inference mismatch introduced by masked-infilling training. 2To the best of our knowledge, WaveGen is the first CFM-based end-to-end waveform TTS model to outperform conventional multi-stage TTS systems on the Emilia dataset. WaveGen also achieves the best performance among the evaluated waveform diffusion TTS models, including WavTTS and BareWave, both of which were released after our NeurIPS 2026 submission. Nevertheless, we acknowledge that WavTTS provides valuable analyses of optimization strategies for waveform diffusion, which complement our findings and offer useful insights into improving the training of waveform TTS systems. 5 Spectral Analysis of Audio Format and Prediction Space
Impact of Audio Compression Neural vocoders and audio codecs are commonly trained on high-
quality waveform datasets, and their training can often be effective even with relatively small datasets.
By contrast, modern TTS models require large-scale training datasets to model diverse speaking
styles including prosody and timbre in zero-shot scenarios. Although Emilia enables large-scale
training, its MP3-compressed audio can limit the amount of recoverable high-frequency detail, which
is particularly important for end-to-end waveform generation. As a result, models trained on such
data tend to struggle with generating high-frequency components above 8 kHz. In contrast, models
trained on LibriTTS preserve and generate richer high-frequency information as illustrated in Figure
2. This observation highlights the importance of carefully curating training data for E2E TTS, where
the model must directly learn both linguistic alignment and high-fidelity waveform generation.

sections.title: 6 Potential Broader Impact
sections.content: Societal Positive Impact Our work proposes an E2E TTS model that directly generates high-quality waveform from text, thereby simplifying existing complex multi-stage TTS pipelines and enhancing training and inference efficiency. This efficient simplification, which enables speech generation with single model without relying on external modules, enhances the accessibility of speech technologies and provides foundation for broader adoption in both academic and industrial settings. Furthermore, in terms of application technology, this method can have positive impact on diverse fields such as voice interfaces, education, and media content. In particular, the generation of clear and natural speech can improve the user experience and contribute to the advancement of speech language model. Societal Negative Impact Although the model and method proposed in this work do not directly raise ethical issues, there is possibility of misuse when combined with voice cloning due to their ability to generate high-quality speech. For example, the model could be used to imitate specific speakers voice or generate realistic fake speech to convey misleading information, which may lead to issues such as voice phishing or impersonation. To mitigate these potential risks, it is necessary to pursue complementary research on fake audio detection as well as speech safety, including methods for identification and authenticity verification. As part of future work, we plan to further explore watermarking and authentication techniques to enable tracing the origin of generated audio. Limitation We introduce an E2E TTS model that does not rely on any external modules, including SSL models. Nevertheless, SSL-based guidance, such as REPA, can be incorporated to accelerate training. Due to limited computational resources, we restrict large-scale training to four epochs. The observed scaling trend suggests that longer training may further improve performance, which we leave for future work. In addition, we plan to extend our model to 48 kHz waveform generation.

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: We proposed WaveGen, fully E2E diffusion-based text-to-waveform TTS system. Unlike previous TTS systems, WaveGen directly generates raw waveforms from text without separately trained intermediate representations. By introducing Spectral Forcing, disentangled DiT heads, and multi-scale spectral v-loss, WaveGen enables stable CFM-based optimization in the high-resolution waveform domain. Our results show that direct text-to-waveform generation can achieve promising zero-shot TTS performance and benefit from model and dataset scaling, suggesting simple and scalable alternative to increasingly complex cascaded TTS pipelines.

sections.title: B Implementation Details for Baselines
sections.content: Spark-TTS Spark-TTS3 [59] is an LLM-based zero-shot TTS with BiCodec, single-stream speech codec that represents speech with semantic tokens for linguistic content and global tokens for speaker attributes. TadiCodec-AR TaDiCodec4 [60] is text-aware diffusion speech tokenizer that compresses speech into low frame rate discrete representation using diffusion autoencoder with text-guided decoding. F5-TTS F5-TTS [5] is non-autoregressive zero-shot TTS model based on flow matching with Diffusion Transformer. It removes explicit duration modeling and phoneme-level alignment by padding text tokens to the speech length, and uses ConvNeXt-based text refinement to improve alignment robustness. For evaluation, we utilize the official implementation and released checkpoint.5 ZipVoice ZipVoice6 [77] is compact zero-shot TTS model based on flow matching. It employs Zipformer-based text encoder and vector-field estimator, uses average upsampling for initial speechtext alignment, and introduces flow distillation to reduce the number of sampling steps. CosyVoice2 CosyVoice27 [13] is an LLM-based TTS model with chunk-aware causal flow matching decoder. It improves speech token utilization with FSQ and supports both streaming and non-streaming synthesis within unified framework. CosyVoice3 CosyVoice3 [14] extends CosyVoice2 toward in-the-wild multilingual zero-shot TTS through larger-scale pre-training, supervised multi-task speech tokenizer, and RL post-training. In our comparison, CosyVoice3-RL refers to the reward-optimized with differentiable reward optimization. For evaluation, we utilize the official implementation and released checkpoint. Qwen3-TTS Qwen3-TTS [22] is an LLM-based TTS system built on the Qwen3 backbone. It employs 12Hz speech tokenizer with multi-codebook RVQ consisting of 16 codebooks to represent both semantic and acoustic information. To efficiently model the multi-codebook sequence, it adopts multi-token prediction decoding. For evaluation, we utilize the official implementation and evaluate both the 0.6B and 1.7B checkpoints.9 MOSS-TTS MOSS-TTS10 [18] employs the MOSS-Audio-Tokenizer to convert waveform into unified sequence of discrete representations capturing both semantic and acoustic information. VibeVoice VibeVoice [46] is long-form and multi-speaker TTS model designed to generate expressive conversational speech from text. It employs continuous speech tokenizers operating at low frame rate and uses next-token diffusion to autoregressively generate continuous speech representations. They release their open-source implementation11 and real-time model12. sections.title: C Evaluation Details
sections.content: Figure 3: MOS interfaces WER We calculate word error rate (WER) using open-source automatic speech recognition model, Whisper [50]. We utilize the official implementation of Whisper-large-v314 to evaluate speech intelligibility. SIM For evaluating speaker similarity quality, we utilized WavLM-large which is fine-tuned by speaker verification task15. We calculate cosine similarity between prompt and generated samples. DNSMOS To assess the naturalness of the synthetic samples, we utilized the open-source Mean Opinion Score (MOS) prediction model, DNSMOS16[51]. Crowdsourcing Details We conducted Mean Opinion Score (MOS) evaluations using Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk)17 to qualitatively assess the quality of synthesized speech from the TTS. Specifically, we carried out two types of evaluations: nMOS, which measures the naturalness of the generated speech, and sMOS, which measures the similarity of the generated speaker timbre to that of the prompt speaker. For each evaluation, 20 native speakers of American English participated. Each participant rated 100 samples per model on 5-point scale ranging from 1 to 5. To reduce unreliable responses, such as participants randomly selecting scores, and to improve the reliability of the MTurk evaluation, we included Gaussian-noise samples as control samples. Responses from participants who failed to identify these samples as fake were excluded from the final analysis. sections.title: E Additional results
sections.content: Table 14 shows the objective evaluation results of each model with respect to the number of training steps. The results indicate that model performance consistently improves as the number of training steps increases. Due to limited computational resources, we trained the model only up to 1.1M steps, corresponding to four epochs on the Emilia dataset. Nevertheless, WaveGen-B continued to improve with additional training steps, as shown in Table 15. These results suggest that end-to-end TTS models have strong potential for further improvement with larger-scale training. Table 16 shows the effect of CFG on the WaveGen-B model. Increasing the CFG scale substantially improves intelligibility, reducing WER from 4.26 to 1.77 when the CFG scale is increased from 0.5 to 2.0. Speaker similarity also improves consistently up to CFG 3.0, indicating that stronger conditioning helps the model better preserve the target speaker characteristics. However, excessively large CFG values slightly degrade perceptual quality, as reflected by the decrease in DNSMOS at CFG 3.0 and 4.0. These results show that CFG provides an effective trade-off between intelligibility, speaker similarity, and audio quality, with CFG 2.0 achieving the best overall balance in our experiments.

sections.title: F Multilingual WaveGen
sections.content: Figure 4: Spectral Dropout We conducted multilingual text-to-speech comparison using Emilia (EN and ZH) datasets. For fair comparison, we utilize the same architecture of F5-TTS to demonstrate the effectiveness of waveform-level diffusion training and Spectral Forcing. Then, we adopt the time scheduling methods of WavTTS to compare the effect of Spectral Forcing. For efficient waveform generation, we employ 50Hz resolutions using hop size of 480 for 24 kHz waveform diffusion. F.1 Spectral Loss Basically, we introduce multi-scale spectral v-loss for our models. However, we adopt multi-scale Mel-spectrogram x-loss to compare Spectral Forcing based on WavTTS implementation. We observe that multi-scale Mel-spectrogram loss could improve the initial alignment learning and entire objective performances including WER and SIM. However, this loss induces buzzing sound on the generated waveform. To address this perceptual limitation, we released the perceptually-improved models together using multi-scale spectral v-loss which could significantly improve the perceptual quality. While it shows lower performance in objective metrics, we highly recommend adopting our new objectives for perceptual quality. We released the model finetuned with multi-scale spectral v-loss for perceptually improved speech synthesis. F.2 Spectral Dropout We further investigated the use of spectral dropout in spectral forcing to improve robustness to noise in multilingual datasets. Figure 4 presents the objective evaluation metrics for different spectral dropout rates. The results suggest that higher dropout rates can improve initial alignment when training on noisy waveforms, but may also cause the spectral path to collapse during training. Without spectral dropout, the model tends to rely on the noisy Mel-spectrogram for waveform reconstruction. We therefore selected dropout rate of 0.2 to reduce this reliance while maintaining the stability of the spectral path. F.3 Sampling Steps With large-scale training, Table 17 shows that the model achieves better performance across all evaluated NFEs than that reported in Table 11. Furthermore, we plan to release an accelerated version of WaveGen that enables efficient speech synthesis in only few sampling steps.
